Explain the Single Responsibility Principle in a way that isn't "a class does one thing".

A class should have one reason to change: it should serve one actor or stakeholder. Employee.calculatePay() (finance) and Employee.reportHours() (HR) in one class is the known example: a shared helper changed for one team can break the other's numbers. So the test isn't the count of methods, but who could request a change.
Does the Open/Closed Principle mean code can never be edited?

No. Bugs get fixed and code gets refactored. It means that adding a new variant shouldn't require editing stable code. You can't be closed against every change, so you choose where based on what has actually varied. A good answer mentions both sides: abstraction costs indirection, so add it when a second or third variation appears.
Why does Square extends Rectangle violate LSP? How do you recognize violations?

Rectangle's implied contract is that setting width leaves height alone. Square breaks it, so code correct for a Rectangle fails with a Square. Signs of a violation: UnsupportedOperationException in an override, instanceof checks, subclass methods doing nothing, tighter input checks, or exceptions the base doesn't declare. The fix is to separate the types or make them immutable.
Dependency Inversion vs Dependency Injection vs Inversion of Control?

DIP is a design principle: depend on abstractions, with the interface owned by the high-level module. IoC is a broader idea: the framework controls the flow and calls your code. DI is a technique: objects receive dependencies from outside, in Spring through constructor injection. You can do DI and still violate DIP, if you inject a concrete vendor class.
When is duplication better than DRY?

When two pieces of code look alike but represent different knowledge. Merging them couples unrelated changes, and the shared code fills up with flags. Common example: one DTO reused for create, update and response, until each needs different validation. A reasonable rule is to wait until the third occurrence, and to be sure they change together.
Composition vs inheritance: why prefer composition?

Inheritance exposes parent internals, fixes the relationship at compile time, and subclasses can break when the parent changes (the "fragile base class"). The JDK has known mistakes: Stack extends Vector and Properties extends Hashtable. Composition hides internals, allows swapping at run time, and is easy to test with mocks. Use inheritance for a true is-a relationship where LSP holds. In Effective Java, the example is a counting HashSet subclass that double-counts because addAll calls add.
Aggregation vs composition?

Both are whole-part. In aggregation, parts exist independently: a Team and Player. In composition, the whole owns the lifetime: an Order and its OrderLines. In JPA, composition is cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true. Aggregation has no cascade delete.
List the ways to implement a Singleton and their trade-offs.

Form | Lazy | Thread-safe | Note
Eager static | No | Yes | Simple
synchronized method | Yes | Yes | Lock on every call
Double-checked locking | Yes | Needs volatile | Verbose
Holder class | Yes | Yes | Best general form
Enum | No | Yes | Safe from reflection and serialization. Can't extend a class
Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

Creating an object has three steps: allocate, run the constructor, assign the reference. Without a happens-before relationship, another thread may observe the reference before seeing the writes from the constructor, and use a half-built object. volatile establishes that ordering. The first check runs outside the lock for speed, and the second inside, since another thread may have created it while waiting.
How can a singleton be broken, and how do you protect it?

- Reflection: setAccessible(true) on the private constructor. Throw from the constructor if an instance exists, or use an enum.
- Serialization: deserialization creates a new object. Add private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }.
- Cloning: don't implement Cloneable.
- Class loaders: each has its own static. There's no code-level fix, so keep it in a shared parent loader.
Is Spring's singleton the same as GoF Singleton? Are singleton beans thread-safe?

No. Spring's is one instance per container and bean name. You can define two beans of the same class. The container, not the class, enforces it, so the class stays testable. Spring doesn't make beans thread-safe. Since all threads share one instance, keep them stateless. Per-request state belongs in method parameters or request scope.
Simple factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory: what's the difference?

A simple factory is a method containing a switch; it's a useful idiom, not a GoF pattern. Factory Method uses inheritance: a subclass chooses which product is created. Abstract Factory uses composition: an object creates a family of related products. Summary: one class with a switch, one subclass per product, and one factory per family.
Builder vs constructor vs setters? What does Lombok's @Builder not do?

Constructors are good for a few required fields. Setters allow an incomplete mutable object. Builder gives readable, validated, immutable construction with many optional fields. Lombok doesn't enforce required fields at compile time; it doesn't validate unless you add that; and field initializers are ignored without @Builder.Default. Combined with JPA, Lombok's @Builder removes the no-arg constructor unless you add one.
Shallow vs deep copy? Why is clone() discouraged?

A shallow copy shares referenced objects, while a deep copy duplicates them. clone() is awkward: Cloneable has no methods and only switches behaviour on Object.clone; it doesn't call constructors; final fields can't be reassigned; and it throws a checked exception. Effective Java recommends a copy constructor or copy factory.

Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade?

Pattern | Interface | Intent
Adapter | Changes it | Make incompatible things work together
Decorator | Same | Add features, stackable
Proxy | Same | Control access
Facade | New and simpler | Hide a subsystem
Why doesn't @Transactional work when called from the same class?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, and the transaction logic runs only when a call passes through it. this.save() goes directly to the target. @Cacheable and @Async have the same problem. Fixes: move the method to another bean (the cleanest), inject a TransactionTemplate, or inject a self-reference. Private and final methods can't be intercepted either.
Output: what does this dynamic proxy print?

Using the Proxy example in the Proxy pattern section, the output is:
before hi
after
hi
The handler prints during the call, and println prints the returned value after hi() finishes. Every method on the interface goes through the handler. So do toString, hashCode and equals, which is why calling proxy.toString() inside the handler can cause infinite recursion.
Strategy vs State vs Template Method?

Strategy: the client picks an algorithm through composition, and it rarely changes during a call. State: same structure, but the object moves itself between states and behaviour follows. Template Method: inheritance fixes a skeleton, and subclasses fill in steps. If behaviour is replaced at run time, it's Strategy or State. If only steps vary and it's fixed at class-writing time, it's Template Method.
How do you select a strategy in Spring without a big switch?

Inject Map<String, PaymentStrategy>, keyed by bean name, or inject a List<PaymentStrategy>, where each has a supports(type) method, and build a lookup map in the constructor. Adding a type then only needs a new @Component. Fail clearly when a key isn't found, and add a test that checks every enum value has a strategy.
How does Observer differ from publish-subscribe?

In Observer, a subject knows its observers (as an interface) and calls them directly, usually synchronously in the same process. In pub-sub, a broker sits between them; publishers and subscribers don't know each other and work asynchronously, often across processes, as with Kafka. Spring's event mechanism sits in between: the publisher knows only the event type, and the context routes it.
What can go wrong with Spring @EventListener?

By default it's synchronous, in the publisher's thread and transaction. A listener exception propagates to the publisher and can roll back the transaction. A listener sending an email may do so for a transaction that later rolls back. Use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) for side effects, and @Async to decouple timing. Remember that events in memory are lost on a crash, so critical ones need a transactional outbox.
Output: what happens with this state enum?

Using the OrderState code above, OrderState.NEW.pay().ship() prints SHIPPED, since NEW.pay() returns PAID. OrderState.SHIPPED.cancel() uses the enum's default body and throws IllegalStateException: SHIPPED can't cancel. Constants with a body compile to anonymous subclasses, so NEW.getClass() isn't OrderState.class, whereas NEW.getDeclaringClass() is.
What is double dispatch, and how does Visitor achieve it?

Java selects overridden methods by the receiver's run-time type, and overloads by the compile-time type of arguments: single dispatch. Calling visitor.visit(shape) with a Shape variable doesn't pick the Circle overload, and wouldn't even compile here. With shape.accept(visitor), the first dispatch finds Circle.accept, where visit(this) has a static type of Circle, resolving the overload. Java 21's pattern switch on a sealed type reaches the same goal directly.
Which patterns did lambdas make simpler?

Strategy, Command, Template Method (pass a function), Observer (listeners), and simple factories (a Supplier). Map<String, Supplier<Shape>> replaces a switch. A class still makes sense when the object has several methods, its own state, or needs a name, such as a Spring bean with dependencies.
What's an anti-pattern? Name a few you've seen.

- God class: does everything.
- Anemic domain model: entities with no behaviour.
- Service locator: pulling dependencies from a global registry, which hides them.
- Golden hammer: one tool for every problem.
- Pattern overuse: a factory for a single implementation.
- Magic numbers and strings, primitive obsession (a String for an email), and exceptions for control flow.
Why not return JPA entities from controllers?

Sensitive fields can leak. Lazy associations either throw LazyInitializationException or, with open-session-in-view, fire extra queries while serializing. Bidirectional relations cause infinite recursion. And any schema change becomes an API change. DTOs give a stable contract. Reading into a DTO projection also fetches only the columns you need.
DAO vs Repository? Do I need a DAO with Spring Data?

A DAO abstracts data access in storage terms, while a Repository acts like a collection of aggregates in domain terms. With Spring Data the interface is enough for most cases. Use a custom fragment with EntityManager or JdbcTemplate for complex queries or batch work.
Where should @Transactional go, and why not on controllers or repositories?

On service methods, because a business operation is the unit of work. On a controller, it would hold a transaction during HTTP serialization and mix concerns. On separate repository calls, each call commits alone, so a multi-step operation can't roll back together. Keep transactions short: don't call remote APIs inside them, since that holds a connection.
Design an LRU cache. What's the complexity? How do you make it thread-safe?

A HashMap plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) for both operations. See the code above. Each node needs its key, in order to remove the map entry on eviction. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove null edge cases. Since get reorders the list, it's a write, so all access takes one lock. The simplest form is Collections.synchronizedMap(new LruCache<>(n)). For high throughput, use Caffeine. It records reads in buffers and applies them later, avoiding contention on each read.
Output: what does this LinkedHashMap LRU print?

With capacity 2: put a, put b, get a, put c. It prints {a=1, c=3}. get("a") moves a to the most-recent end, so b is the eldest and is removed. Without the true access-order flag, it's insertion order, and the map would be {b=2, c=3}.
Design a rate limiter for a REST API. Which algorithm, and how would it work across servers?

Token bucket per client key, as it allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate. On one instance, an in-memory map with lazy refill works. Across instances, a shared store is needed: Redis with an atomic Lua script that reads, refills and decrements. Decide on failure behaviour if Redis is down: fail open for availability, or fail closed for protection. Put it at the gateway when you can, return 429 with Retry-After, and evict idle clients. Avoid fixed windows if bursts at boundaries matter.
Design a parking lot: which classes, and which patterns?

Classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, with Strategy for pricing and for spot allocation. The important part is concurrency: checking a spot and taking it must be atomic. Inject a Clock, which makes pricing tests deterministic. For performance, keep free spots per size in a queue rather than scanning. Say what you'd change with multiple gates and a shared database: a unique constraint or an optimistic version on the spot row.
Design a notification system supporting email, SMS and push, with retries.

NotificationChannel is a Strategy, with one implementation per channel, each an Adapter over a vendor SDK. A NotificationService looks up the channels by user preference. Sending is asynchronous through a queue, as a Command with a retry count. Failures back off exponentially and go to a dead-letter queue. Templates use Builder or Template Method. Idempotency keys stop duplicates on retry. Mentioning a transactional outbox ensures a notification isn't lost if the app crashes after a commit.
Design a Logger class that supports levels and multiple outputs.

Levels use Chain of Responsibility, or a simple threshold. Outputs (console, file, network) are Strategy or Observer: a logger holds a list of appenders. Layout formatting is another Strategy, and async output is a Decorator around an appender, backed by a queue. A logger per name comes from a factory cache (Flyweight). That's how Logback and Log4j2 are organized.
Design an elevator system outline.

Classes: Elevator, Request, Scheduler, Door. State pattern for an elevator's states (moving up, moving down, idle, door open). Strategy for scheduling: nearest car, or SCAN, which continues in one direction and serves requests on the way. A per-elevator pair of TreeSets holds up and down stops. Handle capacity, emergency stop, and concurrent button presses through one event queue per elevator.
You see a 300-line if/else that picks a pricing rule. How would you refactor it safely?

- Add characterization tests, to pin current behaviour, including odd cases.
- Identify the variation, and define a PricingRule interface.
- Move one branch at a time into a class, keeping tests green.
- Replace the selection with a registry or injected list.
- Delete the old code.
Small commits that can each be reviewed and reverted are the main point. If rules change often and are owned by business users, consider a rules table or engine rather than classes.
What do high cohesion and low coupling mean, and how do you spot violations?

Cohesion: how closely the members of a class or module belong together (a InvoiceCalculator whose methods all work on invoice totals is cohesive). Coupling: how much one module depends on the internals of another. You want high cohesion and low coupling so changes stay local. Warning signs: a class with unrelated method groups or a name like Manager/Utils, a change that ripples across many classes (shotgun surgery), classes reaching through getters into others' data, and circular package dependencies.
What is the Law of Demeter ("tell, don't ask")? Give an example.

A method should talk only to its own fields, parameters and objects it creates, not to "friends of friends". order.getCustomer().getWallet().debit(total) couples the caller to three classes' structure. Better: order.payWith(paymentService) or customer.pay(total), so the object that owns the data makes the decision. Fluent builders and stream chains are not violations, because they return the same kind of object.
Layered vs hexagonal architecture: which would you choose for a new Spring Boot service?

For a mostly CRUD service, layered is fine and cheaper. Choose hexagonal when business rules are complex or you integrate many external systems (payment, messaging, third-party APIs): the domain stays free of framework code, adapters can be swapped (REST and Kafka entry points calling the same use case), and core logic is tested without Spring. A pragmatic middle ground: keep layers, but put interfaces for external systems in the domain package and their implementations in an infrastructure package. ArchUnit tests can enforce the dependency direction.
Entity vs Value Object: how do you decide, and how do you persist a value object with JPA?

Ask "if all attributes are equal, is it the same thing?" Two Money(100, INR) are interchangeable, so it's a value object; two patients with the same name are not, so Patient is an entity. Make value objects immutable and self-validating. Persist them as @Embeddable (Hibernate 6.2+ supports records as embeddables) or with an AttributeConverter for single-column values like Email.
Design a vending machine. Which patterns apply?

Classes: VendingMachine, Inventory (slot → product, count), Product, Coin/Note enums, Transaction. The core is the State pattern: IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState, OutOfStockState, each implementing insertMoney, selectProduct, dispense, refund and rejecting invalid actions. A Strategy computes change (greedy over available denominations, failing if exact change is impossible). Mention edge cases: insufficient funds, sold out after payment (refund), and synchronising state changes if multiple inputs can arrive concurrently.
Design a movie ticket booking system. How do you prevent two users booking the same seat?

Entities: Movie, Theatre, Screen, Show, Seat, ShowSeat (status per show: AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED), Booking, Payment. Flow: select seats → hold them for a few minutes → pay → confirm, or release on timeout/failure. Concurrency: make the hold an atomic conditional update (UPDATE show_seat SET status='HELD', held_until=? WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (…) AND status='AVAILABLE') and accept only if all rows were updated, or use optimistic locking with @Version; a unique constraint on (show, seat) for confirmed bookings is the final guard. A scheduled job or TTL (e.g. Redis key expiry) releases expired holds. Patterns: Strategy for pricing (weekday, premium seat), Observer/events for notifications, Factory for payment methods.
Command vs Strategy vs Chain of Responsibility?

| Command | Strategy | Chain of Responsibility
Intent | Turn a request into an object you can queue, log or undo | Swap the algorithm for one job | Pass a request along handlers
Who decides what runs | Whoever created the command; the invoker just calls execute() | The client or configuration picks one | Each handler: handle it, pass it on, or both
How many run | One (or a macro of several) | Exactly one | Zero to all of them
Holds | Receiver and parameters | Usually no state | A link to the next handler
Java / Spring example | A Runnable submitted to an executor; undo stacks | Comparator, PasswordEncoder | Servlet filters, the Spring Security filter chain
Rule of thumb: Strategy answers "how do I do this job?", Command answers "what should be done, and when?", and a chain answers "who should deal with this?".
Mediator vs Observer?

| Mediator | Observer
Shape | Many objects talk only to one hub | One subject notifies many listeners
Knowledge | The mediator knows every participant | The subject knows only a listener interface
Where the logic lives | In the mediator (risk: it becomes a god class) | Spread over the listeners
Flow | Easy to follow: read one class | Harder: who reacts is decided at runtime
Examples | A form controller coordinating widgets; saga orchestration | Spring @EventListener, RxJS subjects in Angular; saga choreography
Rule of thumb: pick a mediator when a fixed sequence of steps must be coordinated and you want it visible in one place; pick Observer when the sender should not care who reacts.
Composite vs Decorator: both wrap components, so what is the difference?
Flyweight vs Singleton vs Object Pool?

| Flyweight | Singleton | Object Pool
Instances | One per distinct value | Exactly one | A fixed set of reusable ones
State | Immutable, shared | Shared; must be thread-safe | Mutable; one user at a time
Use | Many clients share the same object at once | Everyone shares it | Borrow, use, return
JDK / real example | Integer.valueOf cache (-128 to 127), string literals | Runtime.getRuntime() | HikariCP connections, thread pools
Main risk | Comparing with == works only inside the cache | Hidden global state | Leaks when objects are not returned
Rule of thumb: Flyweight saves memory for many identical immutable values, a pool saves creation cost for expensive mutable resources, and a Singleton is about having one of something.
